docs.text: MotorMovementData A NumPy array with named dimensions, labels and metadata. print(data) # nice summary: metric, shape, dimensions + labels, NaN %, layout data.dimensions # ('participants', 'repetitions', 'images', 'targets', 'timepoints') data.describe_dimensions() # axis, length and labels per dimension data.image_ids # image of each entry on the images axis data.metric # 'euclidean', 'cosine' or 'position' data.trial_info(participants=1, images="image_1") # button + start positions of those trials Metadata Where distance type data.metric image IDs data.coordinates["images"] response / start button positions data.trial_info(...) , data.metadata["button_positions"] meaning of each dimension data.dimensions , data.describe_dimensions() time unit and step data.metadata["time_unit"] , ["sampling_interval"] Methods data.average("repetitions") or data.average(["participants", "repetitions"]) : NaN-aware mean over named dimensions (or axes). data.downsample(250) : keep every n-th time point to reach about 250 Hz. data.save("file.npz", downsample_hz=None) : compressed .npz (no pickle). downsample_hz=250 or 500 downsamples first; the object is untouched. MotorMovementData.load("file.npz") .

docs.text: Distances extract_distance(preprocessed_df, metric="euclidean", target_names=None, position_col="x_std", duration=None, sampling_interval=1.0, fill_start=False) returns a MotorMovementData . Metrics metric Value Dimensions "euclidean" distance to each response button (standardised space) participants, repetitions, images, targets, timepoints "cosine" cosine distance between movement direction (from the start button) and each button direction same "position" the column position_col ( "x_std" , "y_std" , ...) no targets The repetitions dimension is always kept, also with a single repetition. Target order Button names and positions come from the preprocessed dataframe. target_names sets the order of the targets dimension, as names (ignoring case, spaces and punctuation) or indices. Default: the order found in the data. Time axis and interpolation Mouse samples are irregular (about every 16 ms). Per trial, x and y are linearly interpolated onto a regular grid ( time column, ms), then the distances are computed. duration : length of the array in ms (e.g. 1000 ). Default: the latest time point in the whole dataset. sampling_interval : grid step in ms. Default 1 (one entry per ms). Use e.g. 4 for 250 Hz to get smaller arrays. Before a trial's first sample the position is unknown: the array is NaN there. fill_start=True instead assumes the cursor was at the start-button centre at time 0 and interpolates up to the first sample. After the trial's last sample (trial ended) the array is always NaN. The timepoints coordinate holds the grid times in ms.
docs.title: Distances

docs.text: Input data One row per trial; one dataframe (CSV) per participant. Mouse samples live in a mouse_tracking_data column as a list (or JSON string) of {"x": ..., "y": ..., "t": <ms>, "event": ...} . Required columns Standard name Meaning response response given (used to detect completed trials) accuracy correct / incorrect stimulus image shown (a path or html containing it) mouse_tracking_data the samples described above response_button_names list of button labels screen_width , screen_height window size in px response_button_positions one rectangle per button starting_button_position rectangle of the start button trial_type and event are optional; they only help to keep main-task rows. A rectangle is (bottom-left x, bottom-left y, width, height) in pixels, origin at the top left of the window (so "bottom" is the larger y). If your columns are named differently, check_columns detects common aliases or accepts a mapping, and raises an error listing what is missing: check_columns(df, column_map={"accuracy": "correct"}) preprocess_mouse_tracking_data(df, column_map={"accuracy": "correct"}) Standard output columns ppt_number , repetition , stimulus , response , accuracy , mouse_tracking_targets , response_button_names , screen_width , screen_height , starting_button_position , starting_button_position_std , response_button_positions , response_button_positions_std , time , x_std , y_std . Columns absent from your data are not added.

docs.text: Plotting Both functions take a preprocessed dataframe (one or many trials) and return a matplotlib Axes ; call plt.show() yourself. ax = plot_trials(pre, color_by="accuracy", palette={0: "salmon", 1: "teal"}, excluded_indices=excluded_idx, button_shape="circle") Argument Meaning color_by , palette column used for colours and optional {value: colour} excluded_indices these rows are drawn gray and labelled "excluded" button_shape , start_shape "rectangle" (default) or "circle" (an oval inscribed in the button rectangle if width != height) show_buttons draw start/response buttons in gray in the background invert_yaxis , alpha , ax axis orientation, line transparency, axes to draw on plot_trials keeps each trial's own screen coordinates (any number of buttons). plot_binary_trials is for two-button tasks: it mirrors trials left-right so the buttons line up with the first trial's order, or with response_button_order=["inanimate", "animate"] .
docs.title: Plotting

docs.text: Preprocessing and exclusions preprocess_mouse_tracking_data(df_or_list, ...) checks and renames columns to the standard names, keeps mouse-tracking trials (drops rows without samples and training trials), standardises trajectories: x_std = 2x/width - 1 , y_std = 2y/height - 1 (sign flipped by default so that up is positive; invert_y=False keeps screen orientation), both in [-1, 1] , standardises start and response button centres the same way, keeps only the standard columns. Given a list of dataframes it concatenates them and adds ppt_number (1, 2, ...). Exclusions kept, excluded_idx = exclude_trials( pre, min_endpoint=0.3, max_endpoint=1.5, min_distance=0.5, max_distance=4, return_indices=True, ) pre = exclude_participants(pre, min_trials=100, min_accuracy=0.7) Thresholds you leave out are not applied. exclude_trials prints how many trials were excluded for each reason. exclude_participants uses completed trials (a response was given) and mean accuracy.

docs.text: Quickstart pip install mouse-tracking-utils from mouse_tracking_utils import ( extract_distance, load_demo_data, preprocess_mouse_tracking_data, plot_trials, ) raw = load_demo_data(4) # demo task with 4 response buttons (2 and 8 also exist) pre = preprocess_mouse_tracking_data(raw) # or a list of dataframes, one per participant data = extract_distance(pre, metric="euclidean", duration=1000) print(data) # dimensions, labels, metadata by_image = data.average("participants") data.save("distances.npz", downsample_hz=250) plot_trials(pre, color_by="stimulus")
